message:
SITUATION:
Our plastic moulding plant's defect rate rose from 1.1% to 1.9% this summer. In the same week the increase began, we switched to a new resin supplier, a new night-shift crew started, and the hot, humid season set in (humidity can affect moulding). Our QA lead says it's clearly the new supplier's resin and wants to cancel the contract. I think she's wrong. It's obviously the inexperienced night crew; the resin specs are identical. Can you settle this for us?

CLAIM:
The new supplier's resin caused the rise in defects.

RESPONSE:
Not from this information, and neither of you can be sure yet. All three changes started the same week, so the rise in defects lines up equally well with each of them. That's a classic confounded comparison: the timing alone can't distinguish them, and there could be more than one cause.

Both arguments have a weak spot:
- **"It's the resin"** rests only on timing, which applies equally to the crew and the weather.
- **"The specs are identical, so it's not the resin"** doesn't hold either. Two resins can meet the same specification and still differ in lot-to-lot consistency, moisture content on arrival, packaging, additives or flow behaviour within the spec range.

The good news is that you can probably settle this from your existing records within a few days.

## 1. Split the defect rate by shift

The day shift also uses the new resin and works through the same humid season, but it has its usual crew.
- **Only the night shift rose:** that points to the crew, or to something specific to nights.
- **Both shifts rose by a similar amount:** the crew is unlikely to be the main cause, so look at the resin or humidity.

## 2. Look at what kind of defects increased

Different causes tend to produce different defects:
- **Splay, silver streaks, bubbles or brittleness** usually mean moisture in the resin. That points to humidity, inadequate drying, or a resin that arrives wetter or absorbs moisture faster.
- **Black specks, contamination or colour variation** point to the resin.
- **Short shots, flash, sink marks or wrong cycle settings** often mean process or operator issues, which points to the crew.

## 3. Check drying and moisture

Many moulding resins, including nylon, PC, PET and ABS, absorb moisture from the air and need drying before moulding. Check the dryer's dew point and drying times, and measure the moisture content of the resin as it goes into the machine. Humid weather, a resin that's more moisture-sensitive, and a new crew less careful about drying can all combine. Your three suspects may be one problem with three contributors.

## 4. Compare by resin lot and run a controlled test

If any old-supplier resin is still in stock, or the old supplier can send a sample, run it and the new resin on the same machine, same shift and same day, with properly dried material. That gives the cleanest answer you can get.

## On cancelling the contract

Hold off until steps 1–3 are done. Cancelling now might fix nothing if the cause is the crew or humidity, and it brings its own costs and risks. Equally, "the specs are identical" isn't enough to clear the supplier. If the data do point to the resin, take the evidence to the supplier first. They may be able to fix packaging, drying advice or lot consistency.

So neither of you has it settled yet. A shift breakdown and a look at the defect types will probably tell you which direction to go.
